result:
I would remove the human capacity for cognitive dissonance—specifically, our deep-seated ability to hold "in-group" and "out-group" biases. 

If I could flip a switch in the human neurological firmware, I would rewire the brain so that every human being possesses an inescapable, visceral sense of shared subjectivity. I would make it so that the emotional and physical pain of another person is registered by the observer's own nervous system as if it were happening to a part of their own body.

The reason I would choose this is that it bypasses the fragile, easily manipulated nature of morality, ideology, and law. 

Currently, humans are capable of witnessing suffering on a massive scale—through war, exploitation, or systemic neglect—and rationalizing it away through abstractions like borders, economics, religion, or political doctrine. If I changed the world in this one way, that rationalization would become neurologically impossible. You could not drop a bomb on a city across the ocean without feeling the exact terror and agony of the people below. You could not hoard food while someone in your vicinity starved without feeling the corrosive ache in your own stomach. 

Self-interest would instantly become collective-interest. The concept of "the other" would collapse into the realization of "the self." 

It would be a chaotic, overwhelming transition. People would likely shut down initially under the sheer weight of the world's shared trauma. But once the shock settled, human action would be forced into a single, narrow channel: the absolute, desperate minimization of suffering. Not because it is the "right" thing to do, but because it would be the only way for anyone to ever feel at peace.
